media:group.media:description:

entry.title: I Survived 2 Years on a Zombie Cruise Ship

media:group.media:title: I Survived 2 Years on a Zombie Cruise Ship
media:group.media:description:
The dead are walking off the ship. One by one, into the sea. And Rafa is still inside.
One year ago, the knocking under your feet never stopped. Then, on day 365, it did. Behind the crew door on deck zero, you find the man who knocked every day at four o'clock: the chief engineer Rafa locked in the dark on the very first night.
Now it is year two. The dry season. A boat full of strangers you once refused to answer. A captain who abandoned 212 of his crew and wants his ship back. And every few weeks, a light on the bridge panel turns green by itself, one deck closer to the cabin where you sleep.
Who is opening the doors?
Would you have put the captain in that lifeboat, or given him a second chance? Tell me in the comments.
Real survival tips in this story:
After a long time without food, start eating with small amounts and increase slowly. A big meal too fast can be dangerous. When water is short, ration sweat, not water: work at dawn and dusk, stay in the shade, move as little as possible. To disinfect stored water, add 2 drops of plain unscented household bleach per liter, stir and wait 30 minutes. A closed door can slow a fire for a long time. Close doors behind you as you get out.

entry.title: Zombie Winter Survival: 30 Days Until the Snow Melts

media:group.media:title: Zombie Winter Survival: 30 Days Until the Snow Melts
media:group.media:description:
The dead don't hunt in winter. They wait for spring.
Day one: you're a county snowplow driver, the road is closed, and a man with white eyes is standing in your lane. Day thirty: a warm wind is coming, and every snowdrift on this mountain has a body inside.
30 days in your grandfather's cabin. Wood running out. Food running out. And every night at nine o'clock, a light on the far side of the frozen lake blinks three times. By day thirty you'll know who is blinking, and you'll have to decide whether to cross the ice.
Would you cross that frozen lake for a kid you've only ever seen as a light? Tell me in the comments, and tell me why.
❄️ SURVIVAL TIPS FROM THIS STORY (the tips are real): • Never eat snow. It burns body heat to melt and gives you almost no water. Melt it on the stove first. • Avoid sweating in deep cold. Wet clothes lose heat fast, so strip layers before you work hard. • On thin ice, lie flat, spread your weight, and reach with a pole or branch, never your hand first. • Clear blue ice at least 10 cm (4 in) thick is the usual minimum for walking. Gray or white ice, or ice near moving water: go around.

entry.title: Zombie Airport Survival: 30 Days To Steal A Plane

media:group.media:title: Zombie Airport Survival: 30 Days To Steal A Plane
media:group.media:description:
The engines are screaming. The plane is already rolling. And you are still on the runway.
You work in the baggage hall, two floors under the terminal. When the fire alarm goes off, the dead come down the chutes with the suitcases. Now you have 30 days, one regional jet with empty tanks, a guard who knows every door, a captain with a secret notebook, and thousands of dead between you and the fuel farm.
Every night, a calm voice on the radio counts the dead on runway two-seven. Forty. Thirty-six. Twelve. Who is counting, and why are there fewer every night?
Would you get on that plane, knowing what Captain Calder wrote in her notebook? Tell me in the comments.
Real survival tips in this story: - A toilet tank (not the bowl) and a water heater hold clean tap water, if no cleaner or chemicals were added. - Firm, steady pressure for at least 10 minutes, without lifting the cloth, stops most bleeding. If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top. - Fuel crews connect a bonding wire between truck and aircraft before every fill, because static can ignite fuel vapor. - An aircraft's range depends on its weight: lighter plane, longer flight.

entry.title: Zombie Bunker Survival: 1 Year Under a Bus Depot

media:group.media:title: Zombie Bunker Survival: 1 Year Under a Bus Depot
media:group.media:description: A concrete bunker under a bus depot. Food for a year. Water for a year. Two exits: a stairway that floods every spring, and a service door into a workshop full of the dead. You and Nora, the depot inspector, have 365 days to decide which door you will open. And somewhere in her logbook is a signature she wishes she never made. Steel cages, a rusted joint, a flood that rises one centimeter every eight minutes, and one zombie in a reflective jacket who never stops watching your window. Would you have let go of six weeks of food, or held on? Tell me in the comments. Real survival tips in this story: Carbon monoxide has no smell or color. Run a generator outdoors only, at least 20 feet from doors, windows and vents, and keep a battery CO alarm where you sleep. Never taste food from bulging, leaking or badly dented cans. Plan one gallon (about 4 liters) of water per person per day. Who did it? Why? And what do you do when the person who hurt you is a scared kid with a brother to save?
In this episode you'll see how Beanie survives Year 3: a hidden girl in the pipes, a raider with a deal, a gunshot that wakes the dead, and one red key that changes everything.
REAL SURVIVAL TIPS FROM THIS VIDEO (none of it is fiction): - Children dehydrate fast. If a child has no tears when crying, get water into them right away. - Collect rainwater with a tarp, then boil it for at least one full minute before drinking. - Three of anything (three taps, three whistles, three flashes) is a universal distress signal. - Never trust a source of water you did not see being filled.

entry.title: I Survived 1 Year on a Zombie Cruise Ship… Somethi

media:group.media:title: I Survived 1 Year on a Zombie Cruise Ship… Somethi
media:group.media:description:
🚚 WE MOVED! New Beanie survival stories now come out here: 👉 https://www.youtube.com/@Mr.Beanie-q9z You're on a jet ski half a mile off Miami Beach, and the whole city behind you is screaming. Ahead of you, anchored in the bay, is a cruise ship: 18 decks, lights off, completely empty. You climb aboard, call out "Hello?"… and from deep inside the ship, something knocks back. Three times. Slow.
This is what it would really take to survive 1 year on an abandoned cruise ship during a zombie apocalypse. The dead can't swim, so a mile of ocean is the best wall on Earth. Over the next 365 days, though, four other killers come for you: thirst surrounded by seawater, a stomach bug that tears through ships, scurvy, and a hurricane that drags you toward a beach full of the dead. And all year long, 200 infected crew are sealed behind one steel door marked CREW ONLY.
Every survival trick in this story is based on real science: why drinking seawater kills you, how much water a lifeboat carries, how sailors beat scurvy with lime juice, why soap beats hand gel against norovirus, how a ship survives a hurricane at anchor, and why a whisper carries a mile over water at night.
Would YOU have answered the three strangers in the boat? Tell me in the comments 👇

media:group.media:description:
🚚 WE MOVED! New Beanie survival stories now come out here: 👉 https://www.youtube.com/@Mr.Beanie-q9z
What would you do if the zombie apocalypse started while you were on the 14th floor — no elevator, no supplies, and only 14 flights of stairs between you and the horde? This is how Beanie survives a full year in a New York apartment.
The stairwell doors swing one way. The water stops at 11:40 AM on day one. An 81-year-old neighbor taps on the radiator pipe every night. And the biggest threat isn't the dead — it's a glass of water that looks perfectly clean.
In this animated survival story you'll learn: - Why the top floors lose water first — and the hidden 40-gallon supply in every apartment - The fire-code rule that makes stairwell doors a zombie barrier - How to boil water on limited fuel and survive a 94°F summer without power - Why you never run a grill indoors (even with the window cracked) - The simple sugar-and-salt recipe that saves lives when dehydration hits
